title: Retiring three services on purpose, and keeping what could not be rebuilt
summary: I removed a game server, a read-only code mirror and a network-boot container in code, and exported the one thing that could not be recreated first.

stat.label: the order that mattered: save the irreplaceable data, verify it, then destroy

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: Every service I run costs attention: updates, monitoring, secrets and review. Three of mine no longer earned it. A game server that had stopped earning its upkeep, a read-only mirror of my repositories, and a container for booting machines over the network. Meanwhile my AI usage was moving to a smaller plan, which made upkeep the thing to cut.

sections.heading: What I did
paragraphs: One pull request removed all three guests together with everything attached to them: their roles and playbooks, inventory entries, workflows, a public route, a secrets role and policy, and a backup hook.

The same pull request added a script to export the game world, and a short runbook for restoring it. The save was the only thing in the whole set that could not be rebuilt from code, so the export had to exist before anything was destroyed.

A reviewer caught that the export script assumed tools and credentials that the machine running it did not have. It now checks its prerequisites up front, names what is missing, and says which machine has them. A second review pass found that destroying the game container leaves networking rules behind on the host, so I added a play that removes them and checks they are gone. It keeps the one setting a host still needs unless you opt in to removing it.

sections.heading: Why this counts as engineering
paragraphs: Removing a service is the same discipline as adding one. A teardown that skips the cleanup leaves rules, secrets and routes that nobody remembers, and they quietly widen what the lab exposes.
The read-only mirror was meant as a backup against losing my hosted code. Once my plan changed, the cost of running it outweighed that risk, so it went too.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: Sort the pile by what can be rebuilt. Code and config are recreated by a pull request, so destroy them freely. The save file is not, so export it, check the copy, and only then pull the plug.

sources: petedio-iac pull request PET-779 (retire Palworld, the Forgejo mirror and the netboot container)
